Article Title: After 28 years, Mirabai Chanu finally puts India back on Asian Games weightlifting podium
Article Text:
Mirabai Chanu and Karnam Malleswari (Image credit: Agencies)

The wait of 28 years

Nagoya brought another chance

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For 28 years, Indian weightlifting waited for this moment. There were new lifters, big names, and fresh hopes of returning to the Asian Games podium. But the medal remained out of reach.On Wednesday, Mirabai Chanu finally ended the wait.With India's hopes resting on her shoulders, the Tokyo Olympic silver medallist lifted 198kg to win silver in the women's 49kg event at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya.It was India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari won silver at the 1998 Bangkok Games.India's last Asian Games weightlifting medal came in 1998, when Malleswari won silver in Bangkok. India did not win a weightlifting medal at the 2002 Asian Games in Busan. The 2006 Asian Games in Doha brought another setback. The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) suspended the Indian Weightlifting Federation following multiple positive doping tests. India did not take part in the weightlifting events after the government failed to pay a USD 50,000 fine to the IWF to lift the suspension.At the 2010 Asian Games in Guangzhou, India sent 12 weightlifters but returned without a medal.Four years later in Incheon, India fielded seven weightlifters. The team included names such as Sathish Sivalingam, Khumukcham Sanjita Chanu, Mirabai and Punam Yadav. But once again, Indian weightlifters returned empty-handed.The 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and Palembang also ended without an Indian weightlifting medal. India fielded four lifters, with Sathish Sivalingam among the senior names and medal contenders.Then came the 2022 Asian Games, which were held in Hangzhou in 2023.There was fresh hope as Mirabai was one of India's leading medal contenders. India sent only two female weightlifters - Mirabai and Bindyarani Devi. Both came close, but India's wait continued. Mirabai narrowly missed a medal at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023. She finished fourth after an injury prevented her from completing her final clean and jerk attempt.When the Asian Games arrived in 2026, Mirabai once again carried India's hopes. She entered the competition with confidence after winning her third straight Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow earlier this year. But the Asian Games presented a stronger challenge, with North Korea's defending champion and world champion Ri Song Gum leading the field.This time, Mirabai made the opportunity count. Mirabai finished with a total of 198kg in Nagoya. She lifted 87kg in the snatch before producing a best lift of 111kg in the clean and jerk. That was enough for silver and ended India's 28-year wait for an Asian Games weightlifting medal.Ri Song Gum won gold with a record-breaking total of 215kg. She lifted 94kg in the snatch and 121kg in the clean and jerk. Indonesia's Luluk Diana Tri Wijayana won bronze with a total of 191kg.For Mirabai, the silver was more than just another medal. She had won an Olympic silver, World Championship medals and multiple Commonwealth Games titles. But an Asian Games medal had remained missing from her collection.And after 28 years, Indian weightlifting was back among the medals.
Article Summary: Mirabai Chanu lifted 198kg to win silver in the women's 49kg event at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya. It was India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari won silver at the 1998 Bangkok Games.

Article Title: India ODI squad to assemble in Thiruvananthapuram by September 24
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Shubman Gill-led India ODI squad for the three-match series against West Indies is set to assemble in Thiruvananthapuram by Thursday (September 24). Some players will reach the venue for the series opener on Wednesday night, while the rest will link up a day later.The series will see Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma back in action, while Ravindra Jadeja will return to the format after being omitted from the fixtures following the ODI series against New Zealand earlier this year. Most of India's first-choice ODI players, vice-captain Shreyas Iyer, Ishan Kishan, Jasprit Bumrah and Axar Patel, are on Asian Games duty in Japan. Their absence opened up slots for players like Ruturaj Gaikwad, Auqib Nabi and even the experienced Jadeja.With Hardik Pandya unavailable for selection, the selectors withdrew Nitish Kumar Reddy from the Asian Games because they are keen to give the young all-rounder game time to build and maintain his bowling volume. Head coach Gautam Gambhir asserted after the T20Is against Afghanistan that Reddy will improve when he bowls more in international cricket and even hinted at the possibility of playing both him and Pandya in the XI."From Nitish's point of view, it's actually a great thing that he's been withdrawn from the T20 format, and he'll get game time against the West Indies as well. We know how important a seam-bowling all-rounder will probably be in a year, and when we go to South Africa. And once Hardik comes back, obviously it's going to be good. Sometimes we could even go on to play both of them in the playing 11," said Gambhir.The series is also important for KL Rahul to again cement his position as the first-choice wicketkeeper-bat in the ODI set-up. The think tank has explored using Ishan Kishan by giving him game time and even the big gloves, but Rahul's consistency in this format has been right up there, and his experience will be invaluable in South African conditions. KL Rahul is currently training at the Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru to prepare for the ODI series.The West Indies team has already landed and will commence preparations for the series.Shubman Gill (captain), Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Ruturaj Gaikwad, KL Rahul (vice-captain), Dhruv Jurel, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav, Prasidh Krishna, Gurnoor Brar, Mohammed Siraj, Auqib Nabi, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Naman Dhir.Shai Hope (captain), Jewel Andrew, John Campbell, Keacy Carty, Roston Chase, Matthew Forde, Justin Greaves, Amir Jangoo, Alzarri Joseph, Shamar Joseph, Vitel Lawes, Gudakesh Motie, Keemo Paul, Sherfane Rutherford, Jayden Seales.

Article Title: Asian Games hockey: Deepika's nine-goal show powers India to 20-1 win over Thailand
Article Text:
Image credit: Hockey India

Deepika's nine-goal show

Thailand find a late goal

India continue their goal rush

Japan next for India

NEW DELHI: Deepika produced a stunning nine-goal show as India continued their dominant run in women's hockey at the 2026 Asian Games, thrashing Thailand 20-1 in their Pool B match at the Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium on Wednesday.The forward and drag-flick specialist converted all nine of her goals from penalty corners as India registered their third straight victory of the competition.The win kept the Sjoerd Marijne-coached side at the top of the Pool B standings.Deepika was the star of the match, scoring nine times in a remarkable individual performance.All nine goals came from penalty corners, with Deepika repeatedly finding a way past the Thailand defence as India dominated the contest.Navneet Kaur added four goals, while Rutuja Pisal completed her hat-trick.Neha, Lalremsiami, Sakshi Rana and captain Salima Tete also found the net as India maintained pressure throughout the match.Thailand managed to avoid a clean sheet only late in the fourth quarter.Supansa Samanso scored Thailand's only goal with a drag-flick from a penalty corner. Her effort took a slight deflection before finding its way into the Indian goal.It was the only time Thailand managed to beat the Indian defence.India had opened their campaign with a 19-0 win over Uzbekistan before following it up with a 17-1 victory over Indonesia.Deepika had also scored a hat-trick against Indonesia, while Rutuja and Navneet also hit three goals each in that match.Sunelita Toppo, Lalremsiami and Sakshi scored two goals apiece, while Ishika and Salima also found the target.India took some time to settle against Indonesia, but Deepika broke the deadlock in the eighth minute after India earned four penalty corners in quick succession.Against Thailand, Deepika once again showed why she is such an important part of India's penalty-corner attack.India will next face Japan on Friday as they look to strengthen their position ahead of the knockout stages.The Indian team are looking to improve on their bronze-medal finish at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games They are also chasing their first Asian Games gold in women's hockey since 1982, when India won the inaugural women's hockey title at the Games on home soil.With three straight wins and 56 goals in their opening matches, India have made a strong start to their Pool B campaign.And after Deepika's nine-goal performance against Thailand, India's attacking threat looks even stronger heading into the next stage of the competition.
Article Summary: Deepika scores nine goals as India thrash Thailand 20-1 in 2026 Asian Games. Navneet Kaur added four goals, while Rutuja Pisal completed her hat-trick. Neha, Lalremsiami, Sakshi Rana and captain Salima Tete also scored.

Article Title: TOI impact: Ayushmann Khurrana read shooter Meghana Sajjanar’s story - and backed her dream
Article Text:
Meghana Sajjanar and Ayushmann Khurrana

Bengaluru:

The power of print has come to the fore yet again.“A year ago, I was pushing my limits but hitting a wall without world-class equipment. Then, a single article in The Times of India changed everything,” international rifle shooter Meghana Sajjanar shared Tuesday.The Bengaluru-based athlete took to social media to reveal a remarkable story of unexpected support that gave wings to her global sporting ambitions. It turned out that Bollywood actor Ayushmann Khurrana had read The Times of India feature detailing Meghana’s challenges with top-tier gear and quietly stepped in to sponsor a state-of-the-art rifle for her.“He didn’t know me. We had never met. He just wanted to see an Indian athlete win on the global stage,” Meghana wrote in her post, which quickly went viral. “That rifle levelled the playing field for me, allowing me to train without compromise and take on the best in the world.”The crucial intervention allowed Meghana to compete at the highest level without distractions. Her legendary grit was on full display in New Delhi, where she won a team gold and an individual bronze at the Asian Championship — while eight months pregnant.After giving birth to a baby girl, she returned to rigorous training in June.She is now gearing up for the upcoming ISSF World Cup in Cairo.On Tuesday, the shooter finally met her benefactor in person. “Today, I finally got to express my gratitude to the man who quietly backed my dreams when I needed it the most. No noise, just pure support for Indian sports,” she expressed.Reacting to her post, Ayushmann Khurrana told TOI that reading about her story left him incredibly inspired. “I am deeply grateful to The Times of India for bringing her journey to my attention. I was genuinely amazed by her talent, determination, and raw ambition,” Khurrana said.“Indian athletes make us incredibly proud on the world stage, and it is our collective responsibility as citizens to support them,” the actor added.“Our sportspersons are the real heroes of our country. I’m just happy I could play a tiny part in her journey and see an Indian athlete get the opportunity to conquer the world."
Article Summary: Bengaluru-based shooter Meghana Sajjanar shared a story of unexpected support. Bollywood actor Ayushmann Khurrana quietly stepped in to sponsor a state-of-the- art rifle for her. Her story quickly went viral and she met her benefactor in person.

Article Title: World body threatens suspension of equestrian federation over failure to hold elections
Article Text:
India’s Hriday Vipul Chheda (PTI Photo)

New Delhi:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Fédération Equestre Internationale (FEI), the global governing body for equestrian sport, has threatened to suspend the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI), citing governance concerns and failure to complete the electoral process within the timeline set by the Delhi High Court.TOI is in possession of the FEI mail sent to the EFI, in which the international body has sought a written explanation by Sept 28. The matter is expected to go before the FEI Board on Oct 13 for possible suspension.The FEI has questioned whether the present arrangement provides for a governing body elected by members under a constitution compliant with India’s applicable sports law, including the National Sports Governance Act.The letter points to the ad-hoc committee constituted by the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) on March 27 to administer the EFI. The Delhi High Court had directed the committee to finalise the federation’s constitution and by-laws within two months and notify elections within the subsequent 30 days.According to the FEI, the stipulated period ended on June 27 without a revised constitution being communicated as approved and without fresh elections being conducted.The FEI has invoked Article 8.3 of its Statutes, under which its Board can suspend a national federation for breaching principles laid down in Article 2, after giving it an opportunity to be heard. The letter specifically refers to Article 2.11, concerning ethics and good governance.The FEI has questioned who administers the EFI, following changes in the ad-hoc panel. IOA removed Col Ashok Yadav (retd) from the committee in May, while panel chairperson Yashodhara Raje Scindia and FEI Director (Governance) Francisco Lima subsequently left the panel.The letter states that the FEI is “currently unable to ascertain which person or body is effectively responsible for the administration of the EFI”.The committee later told the court that completing the electoral process could take 150-160 days because of requirements under the new sports law, including restructuring the federation, preparing the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit roster, holding Athletes’ Commission elections and finalising the electoral college.The FEI has made clear that failure to acknowledge its communication or provide the requested explanation by September 28 will not stop the suspension process. It has also asked the recipient to specify the capacity in which they are responding on behalf of the federation, there.
Article Summary: The Fédération Equestre Internationale (FEI) has threatened to suspend the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI) The FEI cites governance concerns and failure to complete the electoral process within the timeline set by the Delhi High Court. The matter is expected to go before the FEI Board on Oct 13 for possible suspension.

Article Title: Roshibina Devi assures medal after second chance, one win away from Asian Games final
Article Text:
Roshibina Devi assures third successive Asian Games medal

New Delhi:

She wasn't supposed to be in Aich-Nagoya. Not at the Asian Games. Not at her third successive continental event. And certainly not one win away from a place in the women's 60kg sanda final.Naorem Roshibina Devi had lost fairly in the selection trials for the Games, held in Srinagar in June. Her teammate Divyanshi Choudhary beat her in the semifinals and went on to win the trials, earning the original berth in India's wushu squad.Roshibina had accepted her fate. After winning bronze at Jakarta 2018 and silver at Hangzhou 2023, she appeared set to miss her third continental Games.Then came a sudden twist of fate.Divyanshi was subsequently ruled out after the Wushu Association of India (WAI) said an MRI showed a high-grade ACL tear with large effusion. The federation replaced her with Roshibina, reopening a door the Manipuri had thought was firmly shut.And she has made the most of it.On Tuesday, Roshibina defeated Macau's Chu Man Sin 5-0 in the women's 60kg sanda quarterfinal at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall to storm into the semifinals and assure herself of at least a bronze medal.A day earlier, she had beaten Bangladesh's Shika Khatun in the pre-quarters.Now she has a chance to go one step further — and change the colour of her medal.The 25-year-old has already changed colours once at the Asian Games. After her bronze in Jakarta, she ended India's 13-year wait for a wushu silver at Hangzhou, finishing second in the same 60kg sanda event.Now, another medal is assured, gold is her target.Her return to the squad, however, came amid a controversy. Divyanshi, who had beaten Roshibina in the trials, disputed her replacement and alleged harassment, while the federation rejected the allegations and maintained that the decision was solely medical.In other matches involving Indians, Hanjabam Langlentombi Devi finished ninth in women’s Nanquan & Nandao, while Aryan Thakur lost 1-2 to Uzbekistan’s Saydullo Aburashitov in the men’s 56kg sanda quarterfinal.
Article Summary: Naorem Roshibina Devi had lost fairly in the selection trials for the Games, held in Srinagar in June. Her teammate Divyanshi Choudhary beat her in the semifinals and went on to win the trials, earning the original berth in India's wushu squad. On Tuesday she defeated Macau's Chu Man Sin 5-0 in the women's 60kg sanda quarterfinal at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall.

Article Title: How a Nagoya baseball ground was transformed into an Asian Games cricket venue
Article Text:
India's players hold the national flag after winning in the women's final T20I cricket match between India and Sri Lanka in the ongoing Asian Games 2026, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nagoya: On the sidelines of the cricket facility at Korogi Athletic Park, a few Sri Lankan men sat watching the India-Sri Lanka women’s final. Not far away, an Australian kept a close eye on the proceedings.They were not casual spectators. They were among the men who helped turn a baseball ground in a public park on the outskirts of Nagoya into a cricket venue capable of hosting the best teams in Asia.The journey began in late September last year, when the decision was taken to include cricket in this edition of the Asian Games . A little over 300 million yen was earmarked to create the infrastructure, including temporary stands with a capacity of 2,500 spectators.Korogi was chosen because of the size of the facility. The Japan Cricket Association (JCA) also had a head start, having signed an MoU with Sri Lanka Cricket in March 2024, paving the way for Sri Lankan curators to be brought in.At the centre of the operation was Jarrad Shearer, an Australian who has lived in Japan for the past 30 years.“When it was decided that cricket would be part of the Asian Games, Alex Miyaji, the CEO of the JCA, approached me for a role because I had played some cricket back home in Perth and knew Japanese,” Shearer, a sports manager in the planning section of the organising committee, told TOI.The transformation was no small job. The existing facility consisted of three baseball diamonds, with lines of trees demarcating the playing areas. The first task was to clear the trees and level the ground.“We did the pitch and the outfield at the same time. While we were digging a hole to build the pitch, we were laying the outfield. So we created one hybrid wicket and four turf wickets,” said Shearer, who is also a Japanese translator by profession.Gamini de Silva, former curator of Bangladesh’s Sher-e-Bangla National Stadium, and Asitha Wijesinghe, curator of Sri Lanka’s Pallekele International Stadium, came on board. They were joined by a few Sri Lankan-origin residents of Japan who had experience as groundsmen.“While the four groundsmen are from here, Gamini and Asitha took turns to be here to oversee the preparations,” Shearer said.Pitch construction, however, presented one of the biggest challenges.“The pitch construction was interesting because we had a Japanese company doing it and they didn’t know anything about turf wickets. So our planning and instructions had to be spot on,” he said.The pitches were built using layers of gravel, washed riverbed soil and 15cm of local Japanese clay.“While we were testing the clay, we were informed that it was very similar to Pakistani clay,” Shearer said.The surface got its first serious test in May during the T20 World Cup East Asia-Pacific Qualifier, when six matches were played on the hybrid wicket.The plan was to use the turf wickets for the women’s competition, but heavy rain disrupted the schedule.“The heavy rain a couple of weeks ago upset our plans and we couldn’t get the turf wickets ready in time. But we are confident that the men’s tournament will be held on those wickets,” Shearer said.After October 3, when the men’s final is scheduled to be played, the facility will, in all probability, return to its original identity as a baseball ground for local children.For now, though, the men who transformed it into an Asian Games cricket venue can stand on the sidelines and take pride in what they have created.
Article Summary: Australian Jarrad Shearer helped turn a baseball ground in a public park on the outskirts of Nagoya into a cricket venue. A little over 300 million yen was earmarked to create the infrastructure, including temporary stands with a capacity of 2,500 spectators.

Article Title: Jay Meena scripts history, assures India’s first Asian Games soft tennis medal
Article Text:
Nagoya: India's Aadhya Tiwari and Jay Meena (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s Jay Meena scripted history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, reaching the men’s singles semi-finals and assuring the country of its first-ever Asian Games medal in soft tennis.Playing in his third Asian Games, Meena battled past the Philippines’ Sherwin Nuguit in a seven-game quarter-final thriller, winning 4-3 to book his place in the last four.The Indian recovered from a tough start to eventually prevail 0-4, 4-2, 2-4, 5-3, 2-4, 7-5 in a closely fought contest against Nuguit.Meena’s semi-final berth guarantees him a medal, marking a landmark achievement for Indian soft tennis at the Asian Games. He had previously competed at the 2018 and 2022 editions of the Games.The 4-3 victory capped a strong run for Meena, who had earlier defeated Pakistan’s Arain Hussain 4-0 in the men’s singles Group D to progress to the quarter-finals.Meena will now take on the semi-finals with a chance to go a step further and secure a place in the gold medal match.India also added a bronze medal in the women’s skeet team event, with Raiza Dhillon, Parinaaz Dhaliwal and Maheshwari Chauhan combining for 331 points.Raiza and Parinaaz both registered scores of 111 out of 125, while Maheshwari contributed 109 to the team total. China claimed the gold with 346 points, with Kazakhstan taking silver.The podium finish gave India another medal in shooting at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, while Meena’s historic run ensured the country’s first-ever Asian Games medal in soft tennis.India’s campaign also saw two-time Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker advance to the women’s 10m air pistol individual final. Bhaker produced a strong qualification performance to make the medal round, while fellow Indian shooters Suruchi Inder Singh and Esha Singh missed out on a place in the final.
Article Summary: Jay Meena reaches men’s singles semi-finals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Meena battles past Philippines’ Sherwin Nuguit in seven-game quarter-final thriller, winning 4-3 to book his place in the last four. Indian recovered from a tough start to eventually prevail 0-4, 4-2, 2-4 and 5-3. India's first-ever Asian Games medal in soft tennis.

Article Title: India win bronze in women’s skeet team event at Asian Games
Article Text:
Raiza Dhillon of India (AP)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's women’s skeet team of Raiza Dhillon Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal clinched the bronze medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, finishing with a combined score of 331.Raiza and Parinaaz both shot 111 out of a possible 125, while Maheshwari contributed 109 as the Indian trio secured a podium finish. Article Title: Juggling Chess Olympiad prep and a commentary gig in India: The other side of USA's only female GM Irina Krush
Article Text:
The other side of America's only grandmaster Irina Krush

A little girl from Soviet Ukraine

A younger Irina Krush (Photo by Zeljka Malobabic)

You don’t want to look like the fool on the team with Magnus. GM Irina Krush

The cost of commentary

GM Irina Krush's prep before commentating on a game (Photo by Jyotirmoy Halder for TimesofIndia.com)

Eyes on Olympiad

Irina Krush (Photo by Photo by Lennart Ootes)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Any secret sauce?

NEW DELHI: For most of its history, American women’s chess had a very simple relationship with the Olympiad podium. It did not have one. Not once, in over four decades of trying, had the United States women’s team finished among the medals at chess’s biennial team championship.Then, in 2002, Susan Polgar switched her allegiance from Hungary to the United States. Two years later, after stepping away from top-level competition to raise her two sons, she sat down on Board 1 in Calvià, Mallorca, and dragged a young, unheralded American team to silver, second only to China and ahead of a Russian juggernaut that had ruled women’s chess for a generation.It was the first medal of any colour the country had ever won in the women’s category.Bronze followed in Dresden four years later, in 2008. And then, after a wait of 16 years that swallowed many careers, bronze again, this time in Budapest, at a tournament where India finally broke through for gold. Three medals across two decades somehow represented three different eras of American chess.The one name, however, that appears on the scoresheet every single time is that of Irina Krush, the first, and to this day the only, woman to earn the Grandmaster (GM) title while playing for the United States.“I was sort of the main player of my generation,” Krush, who is currently playing in her record-extending 13th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, said with a small, knowing smile during an exclusive interaction with TimesofIndia.com.The story does not begin in America. Krush was born in Odesa, in what was then Soviet Ukraine, and arrived in Brooklyn with her parents when she was five years old. Her father, an amateur player of real quality, taught her the moves.Her first tournament against adults followed when she was six, at the Manhattan Chess Club. She made her first appearance for the United States at the World Youth Championship in Poland at seven. By 11, she was already competing in the US Women’s Championship.At 14, in 1998, she won it. Still, almost three decades on, she remains the youngest champion in the event’s history.Krush’s association with India is a long one too. She fondly recalls playing against a young chess prodigy, Koneru Humpy. In the last few years, her association with India has also included a new part of her profession in chess broadcasting and commentary at the Global Chess League (GCL), a league she participated in during its inaugural 2023 season in Dubai, on a roster built around Magnus Carlsen.“It was a chance to play in the same team as Magnus, and it was like a very special opportunity,” Krush added. “I definitely thought that was like a highlight of my chess career.”But a highlight, in her telling, was never the same thing as a comfortable one. “It’s also — you feel the pressure, right? Because you don’t want to look like the fool on the team with Magnus,” she chuckled. “There are two sides to that coin. But overall, it was a very good experience.”She has not played in the league since. What she has done, for the next two seasons, is commentate on it, first in Mumbai and, more recently, in Bengaluru, watching from the other side of the glass.This time, Krush arrived in India with the 46th Chess Olympiad bearing down on her. For more than two decades, the tournament has been the anchor of her competitive identity, and this year, the games in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, were set to begin just two days after her India schedule wrapped up.The commentary booth, for all it has given her, though, has eaten directly into the time she would otherwise have spent getting ready for it.Asked plainly whether she had found any window to play or prepare between broadcasts, she replied: “So far, no. It’s only been a few days, but it’s been so busy. Today, we were asked to appear at the golf thing. So I had to get up at 7:45 in the morning, go to that. Then I had another nap, and then I just had to go here. So it’s a long day. And honestly, I have not had a chance to do much chess for myself at all.”It is a trade she has made with her eyes open, not a complaint dressed up as one. She had spent the months before India trying to bank the form the broadcast schedule was about to interrupt.“I’ve spent the summer playing tournaments, and I just finished a tournament the day before I came here,” she told this website. “There’s definitely been an attempt to try to get myself into good playing condition.”And on the final day, when the commentators were felicitated on the main stage for being the voice of the league, Krush, who became a grandmaster in 2013, barely lingered after the ceremony. She left the arena almost immediately, the next challenge, the Samarkand Olympiad, already waiting.For someone who has spent much of her career playing chess at the highest level, commentary came without formal preparation.“I never did anything special. I don’t have any training in commentary,” she said. “But, you know, it comes kind of naturally for me to talk about chess. It’s something that’s very easy to talk about and get excited about. I like to watch chess.”Her preparation for the booth is less about learning how to commentate and more about doing what she has always done with chess: looking closely at the players and their games.“You definitely try to do some preparation,” she said. “So, you have ways to fill up, you know, give some context for what’s happening. How are the players doing? So, it just requires a little bit of research, you know, to come up with those nuggets that people will find interesting.”But even that preparation changes as a tournament begins to take shape. “At the beginning, you’re doing more general research,” she further noted. “And after the players have started playing against each other, then you’re already more interested in what’s happening in this tournament. What’s the recent results? Not like what happened one year ago in their other matchups.”“As the tournament continues, you start focussing more. What happened in the first half? How do they do again? How are they overall doing in the tournament?” Krush continued.“The tournament itself becomes more of a focus than their history before. Because it’s all now about, like, now you’ve already seen their recent form. So, you focus more on that. Looking at the games is the best part.”The difficulty comes when the chess stops. “The only challenge is, like, maybe sometimes you gotta fill up the time,” she admitted. “You know, the games are over. For me, it’s like, okay, just commenting on the things that are not as exciting for me. You know, just figuring out what to say.“But when we’re on the chess, it’s the easiest.”The United States are among the leading teams at the Women’s Chess Olympiad, with a squad featuring Carissa Yip, Alice Lee, Rose Atwell and Tatev Abrahamyan, alongside the most experienced Irina Krush.“It’s like a very nice mix of the young players who are really kind of, they’re not even at their peak yet necessarily, but they’re definitely rising,” Krush said. “And then, okay, like there’s me and Tatev, and we kind of bring a lot of experience to the team. Playing for like 20 years or more for the Olympiad.”That depth, the 42-year-old says, is the product of a sport that barely resembles the one she came up in.“It’s much more competitive (now). There’s more incentive to play chess, more opportunities to play,” the eight-time US women’s champion shared. “We didn’t have the kinds of prizes we have at the US championships 25 years ago. We didn’t have an American Cup. We didn’t have a Cairns Cup. We didn’t have the Cairns Queen chess award for the next woman who’s gonna become a grandmaster in America.”The dividend, she adds, is visible in the players coming up behind her now.“A whole generation of strong girls coming up, with Carissa and Alice being kind of the main ones, but also other young girls who are close to 2400 as well,” Krush acknowledged.In Uzbekistan, the US women’s team made a dream start, but its campaign soon lost momentum. A draw against Uzbekistan was followed by a defeat to India, leaving Krush’s team in 14th place in the rankings heading into the rest day.For someone who has now spent two seasons narrating other people’s games for a living, Krush is unsentimental about what the job actually requires.Asked what advice she would give someone hoping to follow her into a commentary booth, she does not reach for a formula.ALSO READ: From uplifting heartbroken team to calling out Chess Olympiad hotel mess: Srinath is India's man to count on “Honestly, there’s just a lot of people who are doing it these days, and everyone brings their own special thing to it, right? So you have different styles. You could be like a top GM and then just start doing commentary. You could be like a different level enthusiast and do commentary,” she concluded, while instinctively running her tongue once again along the outside of her gum. “So I really don’t have any advice except I feel like anyone who loves chess and is pretty good at it can do it. ”
Article Summary: Irina Krush is the only woman to earn the Grandmaster title while playing for the United States. She is currently playing in her record-extending 13th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Krush was born in Odesa, in what was then Soviet Ukraine, and arrived in Brooklyn with her parents when she was five.

Article Title: India’s Hockey teams set for Asian Games in white despite promise of blue jerseys

NAGOYA: At the send-off ceremony for the Indian contingent, Hockey India president Dilip Tirkey had sought to put the jersey controversy to rest.“For the Games, the team will wear blue. That’s the primary colour. There’s no confusion, everything is clear,” he had said. But when the Indian men and women take the field against Indonesia and Uzbekistan, respectively, the primary colour may well be white.In the build-up to the FIH World Cup, the Indian teams’ jerseys had come in for sharp criticism after they moved away from the iconic blue and opted for saffron. The switch was attributed to a ‘scientific’ reason — better sighting of the ball — but it made little difference to the men’s side, who finished a disappointing eighth.At the Asian Games , the promised return to blue has proved more complicated. While Tirkey confidently announced that the teams would be back in their traditional colour, he realised only later that the predominant colour of India’s first-choice jersey was actually white, with light blue on the shoulders and neck, and splashes of gold and orange on the front. The shorts and skirts are also in a lighter shade of blue. The second-choice kit is saffron.“All kits for the Asian Games are routed through the IOA and, by the president’s admission, blue was the colour suggested by Hockey India. But the shade of blue and how it is used is up for debate,” a source said.The choice of colour reportedly did not go down well with Tirkey, prompting an effort to get new kits made.“Given how controversy-plagued Hockey India has been over the past few months, the president does not want the focus to shift away from the teams. That’s why he tried very hard to get new sets of jerseys. But given that they have to come through the sponsors, and the women’s team left soon after the send-off, it was always going to be a race against time,” the source said.
Article Summary: The Indian teams' jerseys had come in for sharp criticism after they moved away from the iconic blue and opted for saffron. The switch was attributed to a ‘scientific’ reason — better sighting of the ball. At the Asian Games, the promised return to blue has proved more complicated.

Article Title: India survive Japan scare, defend lowest five-over T20 total by two runs
Article Text:

Wide-ball drama

Hara-Hinze makes his mark

A bizarre wide call, an intervention from the square-leg umpire and a two-run escape. India’s rain-shortened T20I against Japan had all the ingredients of a far more dramatic contest than a five-over game had any right to produce.With Japan needing eight runs in the final over, Alexander Shirai-Patmore attempted a reverse hit against Axar Patel off the over’s third ball. He was beaten. Japanese umpire Chris Thurgate called it a wide.The next ball produced an identical attempt and, again, wide was signalled.Suddenly, Japan needed only five from four balls. India’s players were visibly unhappy. Then New Zealand’s Chris Brown , the square-leg umpire and a member of the ICC Elite Panel, intervened.After speaking to Thurgate, the decision was overturned and Japan’s equation was restored to six from four.It was the right call. Under the ICC’s guidelines, once a batter attempts a reverse or switch hit, both sides of the wicket are deemed off side for the purpose of judging wides.India still had to survive the over. Axar did, conceding only seven runs, and Japan finished on 30-3, two short of India’s modest 32-4.After two days of heavy rain and a long wait for the ground to become playable in Sano, Japan, India ended up owning an enviable record — the lowest total successfully defended in a five-over T20 — and Japan wondering just how close they had come to one of the biggest upsets in their cricketing history.The conditions had made a mockery of conventional T20 logic. The surface was sticky and slow. The outfield was sluggish. All 10 overs were bowled by a spinner.There were just four boundaries across the entire game.India, asked to bat first, discovered the difficulty immediately. Abhishek Sharma was out first ball attempting a shovel sweep. The rest of India’s top order struggled. Iyer alone managed a double-digit score, making 16 off 12.Japan’s bowlers had done their job. Charlie Hara-Hinze, the 17-year-old left-arm spinner, took 2-17, while the entire attack exploited a surface on which timing the ball cleanly seemed almost impossible.Japan’s chase began badly. Axar conceded only two in his opening over, and Ishan’s direct hit from deep square leg accounted for Lachlan Yamamoto-Lake.At 8-2 after two overs, the game appeared to be slipping away.But Japan refused to be overawed. They took 10 from Ravi Bishnoi’s over and seven from Washington Sundar’s, setting up the extraordinary finish.SCORES: Ind 32/4 in 5 overs (Iyer 16, Hara-Hinze 2-17) bt Jap 30/3 (Washington 2-13) by 2 runs.
Article Summary: India beat Japan by two runs in rain-shortened T20I in Sano, Japan. Japan needed only five from four balls in the final over to win. But a bizarre wide call and an intervention from the square-leg umpire led to a two-run escape.

Article Title: From 'Goa Cannon' to Kerala coach: Swapnil Asnodkar pads up for a new innings

KOCHI: Swapnil Asnodkar once made his name with his fearless strokeplay. Now, Kerala wants him to take on a different challenge: getting its batters to attack with the same conviction that once made him IPL's breakout star.The former Goa batter was appointed head coach of Kerala's Ranji Trophy team on Tuesday, succeeding Amay Khurasiya, who stepped down at the end of the previous season. It is, in many ways, a tectonic shift in Asnodkar's role, who built his reputation as a fearless strokeplayer, and whose coaching career, has more recently brought him into Kerala's system.Asnodkar was appointed Kerala’s U-23 coach last year, and that familiarity with the state’s emerging players was a key factor in the Kerala Cricket Association’s (KCA's) decision to elevate him to the senior job.“I like to thank the KCA for giving me this opportunity. Kerala is a good team and I will give my best shot,” Asnodkar told TOI.Former Karnataka coach Sashikant and former Australia pacer Shaun Tait were among those who applied for the job, but the selection panel believed Asnodkar was better suited to the composition of the current squad.“The selection committee felt Asnodkar would be the perfect fit in the current mix, given that the team has so many young players who have graduated from the U-23 setup,” KCA secretary Vinod S Kumar said.At 42, Asnodkar's task is to bridge that gap between potential and performance across formats. Kerala’s bowling has gained experience with the return of Jalaj Saxena and Aditya Sarwate. The batting, however, remains Asnodkar's concern.“The return of veterans like Jalaj Saxena and Aditya Sarwate has bolstered our bowling. It is the batting that has been the concern,” he said.His prescription is simple: batters must convert their ability into runs, giving the bowlers enough to work with. “My job as the head coach is to ensure that our batters bat to their potential and put the runs on the board, which would give our bowlers a chance to take 20 wickets and put results on the board,” Asnodkar said.Among the young players he has identified are Varun Nayanar and Mohammed Enan. But developing individuals is only one part of the assignment. Asnodkar also wants the squad to move together, a challenge that can become particularly important in a team containing players at different stages of their careers.“There are some talented players like Varun Nayanar and Mohammed Enaan. Very little time on our hands,” he added. Kerala begin their season on Oct 11, with an away game against Jharkhand.Before the IPL gave him a national profile, he was one of the many domestic cricketers working his way at the domestic circuit. His breakthrough came with the Rajasthan Royals in 2008, where Shane Warne recognised something in the right-hander’s attacking game.Warne nicknamed him the "Goa Cannon” with a clear brief: Use his wrists and score through clever strokeplay.For those eight weeks, he became one of the most eye-catching performers in the Royals setup. His form did not last into subsequent seasons, but the imprint remained.These qualities that made Asnodkar an intriguing batter: aggression, instinct and an ability to back his game, are qualities he must now transmit to the Kerala squad.
Article Summary: Swapnil Asnodkar appointed head coach of Kerala's Ranji Trophy team. He succeeds Amay Khurasiya, who stepped down at the end of the previous season. Asnadkar was appointed Kerala’s U-23 coach last year.

Article Title: 'False and defamatory': CSK's Vansh Bedi says he is not the unnamed player in sting operation controversy

NEW DELHI: Delhi wicketkeeper-batter Vansh Bedi has denied any connection with the controversy surrounding a sting operation that alleged the misuse of confidential team information in Indian cricket, saying attempts to link him to the case are "false and defamatory".Bedi, who was part of the Chennai Super Kings (CSK) set-up during IPL 2025 and later played for Central Delhi Kings in the Delhi Premier League (DPL), broke his silence on Tuesday after his name began circulating on social media following an undercover investigation involving former domestic cricketer Rachit Bhatia.In a statement posted on Instagram, Bedi said he was not the unnamed CSK player mentioned during the sting operation and had no involvement in the allegations made by Bhatia.“I categorically state that I am not the individual referred to by Ex-Ranji Trophy cricketer Rachit Bhatia in the sting operation concerning alleged match-fixing involving a CSK player, nor do I have any involvement whatsoever in any such activity,” Bedi wrote.He also said that any attempt to connect him with the allegations was defamatory and that his legal team had started the process of taking action.Bedi said his lawyers were pursuing “appropriate civil and criminal action” against those responsible for circulating the claims.The original undercover investigation did not identify Bedi as the player who allegedly supplied confidential information to Bhatia. However, his name later began circulating online.Earlier on Tuesday, the Delhi & District Cricket Association (DDCA) also responded to media reports about alleged corruption in the Delhi Premier League, calling the allegations "unverified".“DDCA would like to clarify that the allegations referred to in these reports are unverified and have not been established by any competent authority. The Association believes it would be inappropriate to draw conclusions about any individual, player or franchise based solely on such allegations,” the DDCA said in a statement.“Given the seriousness of the matter, DDCA has written to the respective authorities and shared the information that has come to its notice, requesting that the matter be examined through the appropriate established processes.”
Article Summary: Delhi wicketkeeper-batter Vansh Bedi has denied any connection with the controversy surrounding a sting operation. Bedi says attempts to link him to the case are "false and defamatory" The original undercover investigation did not identify Bedi as the player who allegedly supplied confidential information to Rachit Bhatia.

He will be included in the Ranji Trophy camp,” Ankit Chatterjee, Chief Executive Officer of the Uttar Pradesh Cricket Association (UPCA), told TimesofIndia.com.The Uttar Pradesh Ranji Trophy camp will take place at the Bharat Ratna Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee Ekana Cricket Stadium in Lucknow from Friday (September 25).Earlier this year, 28-year-old Dayal sought a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the UPCA and was all set to play for Chhattisgarh in the 2026-27 domestic season. However, the move did not materialise as the UPCA gave him an assurance that he would get the chance to play for Uttar Pradesh again.Dayal has not played any competitive cricket since the IPL 2025 final. With Josh Hazlewood and Bhuvneshwar Kumar , Dayal forged a three-pronged pace attack that played a crucial role in Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) lifting their first IPL trophy. Dayal picked up 13 wickets that season. The left-arm seamer was then retained by RCB ahead of IPL 2026, but he did not join the squad and missed the entire season.RCB director of cricket Mo Bobat said at a press conference: “It wasn't in Dayal's or RCB's best interests to pick him due to his personal situation. ”In the UP T20 League, Dayal was retained by the Gorakhpur Lions, and it is learnt that the Allahabad-born cricketer had also started training with the franchise's retained players. However, he was later not included in the 18-member squad.“He is looking in good shape. He has done exceptionally well in the trial matches and, if given the chance, he is ready to play,” Amit Pal, Dayal's coach from his formative years, told this website.The 2026-27 Ranji Trophy will kick-start on October 11. Uttar Pradesh's first match of the season is against Bihar, starting on October 11 at the newly built Rajgir International Stadium.
Article Summary: Yash Dayal has been included in the Uttar Pradesh Ranji Trophy camp. The 28-year-old has not played competitive cricket since IPL 2025 final. Dayal played a crucial role in Royal Challengers Bengaluru lifting their first IPL trophy.

Article Text:

What do the laws say?

's Law 22.4.1

Law 2.12

India survived a scare against Japan on Tuesday, edging the hosts by two runs in a rain-hit one-off T20 International that was reduced to five overs per side at the Sano International Cricket Stadium.Japan needed six runs from the last four balls while chasing India's 32 for 4. But the match took another turn when a wide call was reversed after protests from India.Left-handed batter Alexander Shirai-Patmore attempted a reverse-hit against Axar Patel and missed the ball, which went well down the leg side. The umpire called it a wide. The same sequence was repeated off the next delivery, with another wide called.The second wide decision was also initially given, but after Axar and India captain Shreyas Iyer protested, the umpire spoke to the leg umpire, New Zealand's Chris Brown, and reversed the decision.The equation then returned to six runs from three balls. Japan could score only three more runs and finished on 30 for 3, with India winning by two runs.The result gave India the record for the lowest total successfully defended in T20 cricket. It was also the first men's T20 meeting between India and Japan.India had struggled with the conditions after choosing to bat. The surface was sluggish and the outfield was slow, making it difficult for the batters to score freely.Iyer was the only Indian batter to reach double figures, scoring 16.In white-ball cricket, a delivery that passes down the leg side is generally called a wide. The rule is intended to prevent negative bowling in limited-overs cricket.However, the rise of reverse sweeps and switch-hits has led to questions over how the rule should apply when a batter moves across and attempts such shots.Thesays, "the umpire shall not adjudge a delivery as being a Wide, if the striker, by moving, either causes the ball to pass wide of him/her, as defined in 22.1.2 or brings the ball sufficiently within reach to be able to hit it by means of a normal cricket stroke."The laws do not specifically mention reverse sweeps or switch-hits, leaving some room for interpretation when a batter changes position and misses a delivery that would otherwise have been called wide.The MCC also sets out when an umpire can change a decision.states: "An umpire may alter any decision provided that such alteration is made promptly and does not contradict Law 20.6 (Dead ball not to be revoked). This apart, an umpire’s decision, once made, is final."
Article Summary: India beat Japan by two runs in a rain-hit one-off T20 International. Japan needed six runs from the last four balls while chasing India's 32 for 4. But the match took another turn when a wide call was reversed after protests from India.

The ILT20 Season 5 Player Auction will be held in Dubai on October 1, with the tournament's six franchises looking to finalise their squads ahead of the 2026 season, which runs from November 21 to December 20.Following the pre-auction signings announced in August, teams will head into the auction with a $1.3 million purse, in addition to any unspent balance from the $700,000 allocated for direct signings and retentions. Each franchise must finish with a total squad spend between $1.5 million and $2 million.Franchises must assemble squads of 18 to 23 players, while adhering to strict nationality quotas designed to strengthen both Full Member and Associate cricket.Each squad must include a minimum of 11 players from ICC Full Member nations, including at least four Afghans and one Irish player. Teams are also required to sign four UAE players, one player each from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and at least one additional Associate player from another ICC Associate nation.Players entered the auction with base prices of $10,000, $40,000 or $80,000, depending on their eligibility and international experience.UAE, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia players all carry a base price of $10,000.Bidding will begin at the player's base price before rising in increments of $2,000 up to $50,000, $5,000 between $50,000 and $100,000, and $10,000 thereafter.Each franchise will also have four optional Right to Match cards — one each for a Full Member player, an Associate player, a UAE player, and a Kuwait or Saudi Arabia player who represented the franchise in Season 4.Once the standard player sets conclude, franchises with vacant roster spots may nominate up to eight players for an Accelerated Set before the auction closes.Teams will be allowed to replace players who are injured, unavailable due to international duty or unable to obtain a No Objection Certificate until the end of the league phase. Mandatory quota players, however, must be replaced from the pool of players who registered for the auction.Season 5 of the six-team, 34-match ILT20 will be played across the UAE from November 21 to December 20.

Article Title: 'This time I lost the battle': England pacer Mark Wood retires from international cricket after years of battling injuries

England fast bowler Mark Wood announced his retirement from international cricket on Tuesday, ending an 11-year career after a long battle with injuries.The 36-year-old played 38 Tests, 70 ODIs and 38 T20Is for England, taking 253 wickets across all three formats.Wood last played for England in November last year during the first Test of the Ashes series against Australia. He bowled only 11 overs before suffering swelling in his left knee, the same knee on which he had undergone surgery the previous year. The injury ruled him out of the rest of the Ashes series, and he did not play for England again.In a post on social media, Wood said the decision came after medical advice and a difficult year with injuries."Although this may not come as a surprise given the past year, it just feels like a natural time at the end of my contract," Wood wrote.Wood has also dealt with ankle and elbow injuries during his career and said he had always tried to return stronger after setbacks."I've always tried to be resilient and come back from injury to prove people wrong and show everyone what I can do. Unfortunately, this time I lost the battle."He added that continuing in Test cricket and one-day internationals was no longer possible."On medical advice, test cricket and 50-over cricket are not possible, so the England dream has slowly been ground out of me over the last year."Wood made his Test debut in 2015 and was part of England's last Ashes-winning team, taking the wicket of Nathan Lyon at Trent Bridge to seal the series victory. He was also one of England's leading bowlers during the 2021-22 Ashes series in Australia, where he took 17 wickets.He played an important role in England's 2019 ODI World Cup-winning campaign at home, picking up 18 wickets in 10 matches. He was also part of England's T20 World Cup-winning squad in Australia in 2022."I got to live out a dream and I hope I can continue playing cricket in some capacity and pursuing other challenges in the future," Wood said.Wood finished with 119 wickets in 38 Tests, 80 wickets in 70 ODIs and 54 wickets in 38 T20Is. He took nine wickets during England's 2022 T20 World Cup-winning campaign, while his 18 wickets at the 2019 ODI World Cup came as England lifted the 50-over trophy for the first time.England men's managing director Rob Key paid tribute to Wood, saying the fast bowler "thrilled crowds every time he got the ball in his hand."
Article Summary: England fast bowler Mark Wood retires from international cricket. The 36-year- old played 38 Tests, 70 ODIs and 38 T20Is for England. Wood last played for England in November last year during the first Test of the Ashes series against Australia.

Article Title: India script history, become first team to register 200 T20I wins after edging Japan in thriller
Article Text:

India reach 200 wins faster than ever

Axar, Washington help India survive Japan scare

NEW DELHI: India scripted another milestone in their T20I history on Tuesday, becoming the first team to register 200 wins in men's T20 internationals, including victories achieved through Super Overs.The landmark 200th win came in dramatic fashion as the world champions survived a major scare from hosts Japan, edging them by just two runs in a rain-shortened one-off T20I at Sano.With the match reduced to five overs per side because of rain, India posted only 32/4 after opting to bat. Japan came agonisingly close in the chase, finishing on 30/3 as India held their nerve to complete a historic victory.India's journey to 200 T20I wins began with their inaugural victory against South Africa in Johannesburg in 2006. They reached 50 wins against Sri Lanka in Colombo in 2017, completed 100 victories against West Indies in Kolkata in 2022 and reached 150 against Australia in Gros Islet in 2024.The latest victory against Japan took them into uncharted territory.India have now registered 200 wins from 291 T20Is, comfortably ahead of Pakistan, who have 174 wins from 299 matches. New Zealand are third with 137 wins from 267 matches, followed by South Africa with 131 from 235 and England with 130 from 233.India's progress through the 50-win milestones has also become increasingly rapid.They needed 83 matches for their first 50 wins, before taking 72 matches to move from 50 to 100. The next 50 came in 70 matches, while India required only 66 matches to move from 150 to 200 wins.The 200th victory, however, was far from routine.The low-scoring contest was dominated by spin, with the damp surface and slow outfield making stroke-making difficult.Japan's spinners troubled India's star-studded batting line-up from the beginning. Charlie Hara Hinze dismissed Abhishek Sharma for a duck, while Ibrahim Takahashi accounted for Sanju Samson, who made 10. Benjamin Ito-Davis then removed Ishan Kishan for three.Skipper Shreyas Iyer top-scored with 16, but India could manage only 32/4 from their five overs, hitting just three boundaries.Japan looked capable of producing one of the biggest upsets in their cricketing history during the chase. Ravi Bishnoi conceded 10 runs in the third over, while Washington Sundar's penultimate over went for seven as Japan moved within striking distance.Washington finished with 2/13, while Axar Patel's experience proved crucial in the final over.Japan needed eight runs from the last six balls, but Axar gave Shirai Patmore and Benjamin Ito-Davis little room to attack. Rain had also left the outfield sluggish, making boundary-hitting even harder.There was late drama when a wide call against India in the final over was overturned after an appeal from Shreyas Iyer. Japan eventually finished on 30/3, falling two runs short.The result gave India their 200th T20I win in their historic first T20I against Japan, adding another landmark to the country's growing record in the format.For Japan, the narrow defeat nevertheless underlined how competitive the shortened contest became as their spinners exploited the conditions and kept India's powerful batting line-up in check.
Article Summary: India become first team to register 200 wins in men's T20 internationals. World champions beat hosts Japan by just two runs in rain-shortened one-off T20I at Sano. Japan came agonisingly close in the chase, finishing on 30/3 as India held their nerve.

Article Title: India survive huge Japan scare, win by two runs in historic T20I

India survived a massive scare against Japan to clinch a thrilling two-run victory in the historic one-off T20 International in Sano on Tuesday, with the run-truncated contest producing one of the closest finishes in the team's T20I history.After being reduced to just 32 for four in their five overs, India had their backs against the wall. But their spinners turned the contest around as Japan were restricted to 30 for nine in their five overs, allowing India to escape with a narrow victory.The result also saw India become the first team to register 200 wins in men's T20Is, including victories in Super Overs.The game had promised fireworks from India's batting line-up, but it was Japan's spinners who stole the show.With the match reduced to five overs per side after a delayed start caused by the wet outfield, Japan used spin for all five overs and found plenty of assistance from the surface.The ball began turning from the very first delivery and India's batters struggled to adapt. Abhishek Sharma was dismissed for a golden duck, while Sanju Samson followed in the next over. Ishan Kishan also failed to stay for long. Shreyas Iyer provided India's only substantial contribution with a 16-run knock, but India could manage only 32 runs from their five overs.The damp conditions made matters even harder for the batters. The outfield was slow and boundaries were difficult to come by, adding to the challenge of scoring quickly.Japan walked off after the innings with plenty to celebrate, having reduced one of the world's strongest T20I teams to such a modest total.Japan needed only 33 runs from five overs and appeared to have a huge opportunity to complete one of the biggest upsets in their cricketing history.But India's spin attack had other plans.Axar Patel, Washington Sundar and Ravi Bishnoi kept the pressure on Japan, exploiting the same conditions that had troubled India's batters.Japan struggled to build momentum and, despite needing just over six runs an over, could not get over the line. India eventually held their nerve to defend the tiny target and win by two runs.The tension reached another level in the final over when a wide call against Axar Patel was overturned after an on-field discussion between the umpires.Alexander Shirai-Patmore attempted another reverse sweep and the delivery went down the leg side. The initial decision was called wide, much to the frustration of Axar and wicketkeeper Sanju Samson.Shreyas Iyer then spoke to square-leg umpire Chris Brown, while the two umpires discussed the decision. The original call was eventually reversed and the ball was ruled not a wide.With the final margin just two runs, the overturned call added another layer of intrigue to an already dramatic contest. Had the original wide decision stood, Japan would have received an additional run and one more delivery in a match eventually decided by just two runs.

Article Title: First gold for India at Asian Games 2026: Harmanpreet Kaur-led women's cricket team beats Sri Lanka in final

NEW DELHI: Harmanpreet Kaur-led side opened India's gold medal account at the Asian Games 2026 on Tuesday, defeating Sri Lanka in the women's cricket final at Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin to end the country's wait for a top-podium finish in Aichi-Nagoya.The defending champions produced a dominant performance in the gold-medal clash, first posting a mammoth 216/3 after opting to bat before bowling out Sri Lanka for just 69 to seal a commanding 147-run victory.The result gave India their first gold and seventh medal overall at the Asian Games , with the tally now standing at one gold, four silver and two bronze medals.Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma and Richa Ghosh were the architects of India's imposing total. Mandhana smashed 79 off 45 balls, while Shafali contributed 48 off 29. Richa then provided a spectacular finish, remaining unbeaten on 49 off just 22 balls.India's batters cleared the boundary 13 times during their innings as they posted their highest-ever total in women's cricket at the Asian Games.Mandhana and Shafali gave India a flying start, adding 99 for the opening wicket before the latter was dismissed for her brisk 48.Mandhana continued her assault and brought up her half-century before eventually falling for 79.Harmanpreet made 19, but Richa ensured there was no let-up in India's scoring rate. Her unbeaten cameo, which included six fours and three sixes, took India past the 200-run mark and set Sri Lanka a daunting target.With the ball, India maintained their dominance. Deepti Sharma (3/6) took three wickets, while fellow spinners Shafali Verma (2/3), Shreyanka Patil (2/9) and Shree Charani (2/13) claimed two wickets each as Sri Lanka were bowled out for a modest total.The triumph means India now have two women's cricket gold medals at the Asian Games, having also won the women's cricket gold for the country in 2023.India had not participated when cricket featured at the Asian Games in 2010 and 2014. Their 2023 title and Tuesday's triumph now put them level with Pakistan, who won the women's cricket gold medals in 2010 and 2014.The men's competition will begin later in the Games, with the Shreyas Iyer-led Indian side scheduled to start their campaign in the second quarterfinal on September 28. India are also the defending men's Asian Games champions.India had entered Tuesday's cricket final with six medals from the first two days of competition — four silver and two bronze — with shooting accounting for five of them.On Day 2, Himanshu Dhillon won silver and Rudrankksh Patil bronze in the men's 10m air rifle individual event. Dhillon finished second behind China's Olympic champion Sheng Lihao, who successfully defended his Asian Games title with 254.2 points, while Patil secured bronze with 230.9.Dhillon and Patil then combined with Parth Mane to claim another silver in the men's 10m air rifle team event, taking India's shooting haul to five medals.India's other Day 2 medal came from Suchika Tariyal, who made history by becoming the country's first Asian Games medallist in mixed martial arts. She was awarded bronze after her semifinal against Singapore's Hui Hoon Teo ended in a draw, with Teo advancing under the competition's tie-break rule after Suchika was around 700 grams heavier at the morning weigh-in.India's first medals of the Games had also come from shooting on Day 1. Elavenil Valarivan, Sonam Uttam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod won silver in the women's 10m air rifle team event before Valarivan added another silver in the individual competition.Valarivan shot 252.4 in the final, finishing behind Japan's Hinata Taichi, who won gold with a Games-record 253.0. South Korea's Ban Hyojin took bronze with 230.4.After two days without a gold, India's women's cricketers finally put the defending champions on top of the podium — and did so in emphatic fashion.The cricket gold also lifted India to seven medals: one gold, four silver and two bronze, providing a significant boost to the country's campaign as the Aichi-Nagoya Games move into their next phase.
